name: The Year in Feasts: How Holidays and Festivals Began
description: From harvest rites and midwinter parties to national days and rock festivals: where our holidays came from and how they changed on the way.

checkpoints.name: Rites of the seasons
checkpoints.note: Farming peoples marked the seasons with rites: the Eleusinian Mysteries in Greece, Nowruz in Persia, Chinese New Year, the Roman Saturnalia and Hanukkah. The Roman calendar tried to keep these dates in step with the sun.

checkpoints.name: Faith and the calendar
checkpoints.note: Christmas was set in the Julian calendar, Eid al-Fitr in the Islamic calendar, and Jewish feasts in the Hebrew calendar. The Maya had their own count, and in Japan Gion Matsuri and Hanami began as ways to honour spirits and blossoms.

checkpoints.name: Feasts and masks
checkpoints.note: The Gregorian calendar fixed the year in 1582. Carnival and the Carnival of Venice let people wear masks before Lent, Halloween grew from older autumn customs, and the Day of the Dead blended Aztec and Christian ideas. Valentine's Day was linked with romance in this age.

checkpoints.name: Nations celebrate
checkpoints.note: Revolutionary France briefly tried its own calendar. Oktoberfest started as a royal wedding party, and Thanksgiving, Bastille Day and Mother's Day became national or family days in the United States and France.

checkpoints.name: The festival age
checkpoints.note: Cannes, Edinburgh's Fringe and Eurovision make culture a festival, La Tomatina and Notting Hill Carnival add street parties, and Woodstock, Glastonbury, Live Aid and Burning Man turn music and art into a gathering of tens of thousands.
